bib.title: The Arcade Learning Environment: An Evaluation Platform for General Agents

question: How can general, domain-independent agents be evaluated across many diverse Atari 2600 games, and how well do standard RL and planning methods do on them?
hypothesis: A train/test split over games (tune on a few, evaluate once on unseen games) gives a rigorous evaluation of general competency.
contributions: ALE: a software framework and challenge problem over Atari 2600 games
An evaluation methodology with training and testing games
Benchmark SARSA(lambda) agents with five feature sets and two search agents (breadth-first, UCT) on 55 games
Normalisation and aggregation metrics for cross-game comparison

method.summary: ALE wraps the Stella Atari 2600 emulator as an RL environment. Five SARSA(lambda) linear agents (Basic, BASS, DISCO, LSH, RAM features) and two search agents (full-tree BFS, UCT using the emulator as a model) are tuned on five games and evaluated on 50 test games, with baselines Random, Const, Perturb and a beginner human.
method.task: Atari 2600 game playing (RL and planning benchmark)

datasets.name: Training games
datasets.size: 5 games: Asterix, Beam Rider, Freeway, Seaquest, Space Invaders
datasets.split: used for parameter tuning and design refinements

datasets.name: Test games
datasets.split: chosen at random from 123 eligible of 381 games listed on Wikipedia (July 12, 2012)
datasets.preprocessing: eligible: own Wikipedia page, single player mode, not adult-themed or prototype, emulable in ALE

models.name: SARSA(lambda) with linear function approximation, replacing traces, epsilon-greedy
models.architecture: linear value function over hand-built features

other.Basic: binary feature per colour (128) per tile (16x14 grid) = 28,672 features
other.BASS: Basic plus pairwise feature combinations, 8-colour SECAM encoding
other.DISCO: object class detection, tile coding of position and velocity
other.LSH: locality sensitive hashing of screens, l=2000 random vectors
other.RAM: 1024 RAM bits plus pairwise AND of every bit pair

other.node limit: max 100,000 simulation steps per frame (text) / 133,000 frames emulated per action (Appendix C)

models.name: UCT
models.architecture: Monte Carlo tree search with duplicate-state action pruning and tree reuse

models.name: Random, Const, Perturb, beginner human
models.architecture: Random picks random action every frame; Const best single fixed action; Perturb fixed action with prob 0.95 else uniform random (best per game); human: five-episode average of a beginner

training.objective: SARSA(lambda) TD control, linear function approximation

other.class discovery: 36,000 sample screens, max 10 classes, max velocity 8 pixels, min frequency 20%
other.UCT: 500 simulations per action, max depth 300 frames, exploration constant 0.1

inference.samples: RL: 30 trials x 500 evaluation episodes (no learning); search: 10 episodes per game

metrics.name: Average evaluation score
metrics.definition: mean game score over evaluation episodes

metrics.name: Baseline-normalised score
metrics.definition: (s - min ref)/(max ref - min ref) with range from 37 baseline agents (Random, Const per action, Perturb per action)

metrics.name: Inter-algorithm score
metrics.definition: normalised to min and max over the algorithms compared; in [0,1]

metrics.name: Paired tests
metrics.definition: per game two-tailed Welch t-test with 99% confidence intervals; count of games better-worse

eval.protocol: Tune on 5 training games, evaluate once on 50 test games; average, median and score-distribution aggregates.

availability.code: open source, GNU GPL, http://arcadelearningenvironment.org; benchmark agent source on publication page

limits: Human baseline is a single beginner, five-episode average, selected games only; the authors say it is not exhaustive or accurate.
Test games chosen from games with Wikipedia pages; no estimate of variance beyond 30 trials for RL and 10 episodes for search.
Search agents use the emulator as a perfect model and take about 15 seconds per action, so are not real-time or comparable with model-free learners.
Hand-designed features, linear SARSA(lambda); no deep networks (dated by later work).
Authors concede that cross-game score summarisation needs further attention and that sparse-reward games need long-term planning beyond these methods.
